intro_text:
The Kingdom of Georgia, also known as the Georgian Empire, was a medieval Eurasian monarchy that was founded in c. 1008 AD. It reached its Golden Age of political and economic strength during the reign of King David IV and Queen Tamar the Great from the 11th to 13th centuries. Georgia became one of the pre-eminent nations of the Christian East, and its pan-Caucasian empire and network of tributaries stretched from Eastern Europe to Anatolia and northern frontiers of Iran. At the height of its influence, Georgia also maintained several important religious centers abroad, such as the Bachkovo Monastery in Bulgaria, Monastery of the Cross in Jerusalem and the Monastery of Iviron in Greece. It is the principal historical precursor of present-day Georgia.
The Kingdom of Georgia emerged in the early 11th century through the unification of several Georgian kingdoms, most notably the Kingdom of the Iberians and the Kingdom of Abkhazia. It was governed under a feudal system most closely resembling those of Western Europe. Georgia repelled invasions by the Byzantine Empire and the Seljuk Turks, eventually establishing its dominance over much of the South Caucasus. The kingdom came under Mongol influence in the 1240s but managed to reassert its sovereignty by the 1330s. The following decades were marked by the Black Death and numerous invasions led by Timur, which caused significant damage to the country's economy, population, and urban centres. The kingdom's geopolitical position deteriorated further following the Ottoman conquest of the Byzantine Empire and the Empire of Trebizond. As a result of these developments, Georgia had become politically fragmented by the end of the 15th century. This series of events ultimately led to the final collapse of the kingdom into anarchy by 1466.
